s: A 58-year-old man has had painless, gradually enlarging swelling of the right hemiscrotum for 6 months. The swelling is smooth and soft, and the testis cannot be felt separately within it. A penlight held behind the scrotum makes the whole swelling glow red. The swelling does not change in size when he lies down.
l: Fluid has most likely collected within which structure?
e: A **hydrocele** is a collection of serous fluid in the **tunica vaginalis**, the peritoneal sac that wraps the front and sides of the testis. Because the fluid is clear, light passes through, the swelling transilluminates, and the testis sits within it and cannot be separated from it. In infants a patent processus vaginalis causes a communicating hydrocele; in adults the fluid is usually noncommunicating, and a new hydrocele deserves an ultrasound to exclude a tumor. The albuginea is the testicular capsule, the dartos is scrotal wall muscle, a spermatocele is separable, and varicocele veins do not transilluminate.

w.Tunica albuginea: The tunica albuginea is the tough fibrous capsule of the testis itself; fluid does not collect within it, and a tear of it signals testicular rupture after trauma.
w.Dartos fascia: The dartos is the smooth muscle layer of the scrotal wall that wrinkles in the cold; fluid within it would cause diffuse wall edema rather than a glowing swelling around the testis.
w.Epididymal head: A cyst at the epididymal head, a spermatocele, also transilluminates, but it lies above and behind the testis and can be felt separately, whereas here the testis cannot be felt apart.
w.Pampiniform plexus: Dilated pampiniform veins form a varicocele, a bag of worms that fills on standing and does not transilluminate because blood absorbs the light.

et: Smooth muscle of the scrotal wall
bl: A hydrocele is serous fluid within the tunica vaginalis that transilluminates; a new adult hydrocele needs ultrasound to exclude a tumor.

pt.say: The hydrocele row shows serous fluid in the tunica vaginalis around the testis, and that clear fluid is why the swelling transilluminates.

s: A 16-year-old boy comes to the emergency department 3 hours after sudden severe left scrotal pain that woke him from sleep, with nausea and one episode of vomiting. He has no urinary symptoms and no history of trauma. His temperature is 37.2 °C. The left testis is high in the scrotum with a horizontal lie, and stroking the left inner thigh does not elevate it. Urinalysis is normal. Scrotal ultrasonography is available but would take about 90 minutes.
l: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Emergency surgery to untwist the cord and fix both testes
Scrotal elevation, ice and analgesics with outpatient review
Scrotal Doppler ultrasonography before any intervention
Manual detorsion and discharge if the pain improves
e: Sudden severe pain with nausea, a high-riding horizontal testis and an absent cremasteric reflex in an adolescent is **testicular torsion** until proven otherwise. Twisting compresses the thin-walled veins before the arteries, so the testis congests and then undergoes hemorrhagic infarction; salvage exceeds 90 percent within 6 hours and falls below 10 percent after 24 hours. He needs **emergency surgery** to untwist the cord, and the surgeon fixes both testes because the bell-clapper defect is usually bilateral. Imaging must not delay exploration, antibiotics treat epididymitis, supportive care suits a torsed appendix testis, and manual detorsion only buys time.

w.Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral doxyc: Ceftriaxone with doxycycline treats epididymitis from chlamydia and gonorrhea, which begins gradually with urethral symptoms, a normal lie and a preserved cremasteric reflex; this boy has none of that.
w.Scrotal elevation, ice and analgesics wi: Rest, elevation and analgesics suit a torsed appendix testis, which is focal and subacute and leaves the cremasteric reflex intact; waiting here would risk infarction of the testis within hours.
w.Scrotal Doppler ultrasonography before a: Doppler can support the diagnosis, but waiting 90 minutes spends much of the salvage window, and this typical clinical picture justifies exploration without it.
w.Manual detorsion and discharge if the pa: Manual detorsion can temporize, but pain relief does not prove complete untwisting and the bell-clapper defect remains, so surgical exploration and fixation are still required.

et: Emergency surgery to untwist the cord and fix both testes
Scrotal elevation, ice and analgesics with outpatient review
Scrotal Doppler ultrasonography before any intervention
Diagnostic aid when suspicion is low or intermediate
Manual detorsion and discharge if the pain improves
bl: Suspected torsion needs immediate surgical exploration, untwisting and bilateral orchiopexy; do not wait for imaging.

pt.say: The torsion column shows a high, horizontal testis, an absent cremasteric reflex and treatment by surgery in hours, so emergency surgery, not imaging or antibiotics, is the next step.

s: A 23-year-old sexually active man has had 3 days of gradually increasing right scrotal pain with dysuria and a mucoid urethral discharge. He is afebrile. The right epididymis is swollen and tender, the testis lies normally, and stroking the inner thigh elevates the testis. Lifting the testis eases the pain. A scrotal Doppler ultrasound is performed.
l: Which Doppler finding is most likely?
o: Increased blood flow to the epididymis and testis
Absent blood flow within the testis
Normal flow with a solid intratesticular mass
Normal flow with a small avascular upper-pole nodule
Dilated veins that enlarge on Valsalva
e: Gradual onset, urethral discharge, a tender epididymis, a normal testis position, an intact cremasteric reflex and relief when the testis is lifted (Prehn sign) point to **epididymitis** from Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae in a man younger than 35. Inflammation raises perfusion, so Doppler shows **increased flow** around the epididymis and testis. Absent flow would mean torsion, a solid lesion with normal flow would suggest a tumor, an avascular nodule at the upper pole would be a torsed appendix testis, and dilated veins would be a varicocele.

w.Absent blood flow within the testis: Absent flow marks torsion, in which twisting of the cord closes first the veins and then the arteries; the gradual onset, discharge, normal lie and intact reflex argue against it.
w.Normal flow with a solid intratesticular: A solid intratesticular lesion with normal flow suggests a germ cell tumor, which is painless and comes without urethral discharge or a tender epididymis.
w.Normal flow with a small avascular upper: A small avascular nodule at the upper pole is a torsed appendix testis, which causes focal pain in boys around 7 to 12 years, not diffuse epididymal tenderness with discharge in an adult.
w.Dilated veins that enlarge on Valsalva: Dilated veins that enlarge with Valsalva or standing describe a varicocele, which is typically painless and left-sided, without discharge or epididymal tenderness.

et: Increased blood flow to the epididymis and testis
Absent blood flow within the testis
Normal flow with a solid intratesticular mass
Normal flow with a small avascular upper-pole nodule
Dilated veins that enlarge on Valsalva
bl: Epididymitis shows gradual pain, an intact cremasteric reflex, relief on lifting the testis and increased Doppler flow.

pt.say: In the Doppler flow row, epididymitis shows increased flow whereas torsion shows absent or reduced flow, and the Prehn sign relief and present cremasteric reflex sit in the same epididymitis column.

s: A 68-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia had an indwelling urinary catheter removed 5 days ago. He now has 2 days of fever and gradually increasing left scrotal pain. The left epididymis is swollen and tender, the testis lies normally, and the cremasteric reflex is present. Urinalysis shows pyuria, and a Gram stain of the urine shows gram-negative rods. A nucleic acid amplification test of urine for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis is negative.
l: Which is the most appropriate antimicrobial therapy?
e: In men older than 35, and in men with urinary obstruction or recent instrumentation, epididymitis usually ascends from the urinary tract and is caused by enteric gram-negative rods such as Escherichia coli. Gram-negative rods in the urine and a negative test for chlamydia and gonorrhea confirm that pattern. CDC guidance for epididymitis likely caused by enteric organisms is **levofloxacin**, a fluoroquinolone with good tissue penetration; ceftriaxone with doxycycline is reserved for sexually transmitted cases in younger men. Benzathine penicillin, metronidazole and nitrofurantoin neither cover this pathogen nor reach the epididymis.

w.Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline: This regimen covers gonorrhea and chlamydia, the usual causes under age 35; this man is older, has had catheter instrumentation, has gram-negative rods in the urine and tested negative for both infections.
w.Penicillin G benzathine: Benzathine penicillin treats syphilis and does not cover gram-negative enteric bacilli, so it would leave the likely pathogen untreated.
w.Metronidazole: Metronidazole targets anaerobes and protozoa such as Trichomonas and is not first-line for epididymitis caused by enteric gram-negative rods.
w.Nitrofurantoin: Nitrofurantoin reaches useful levels only in urine and is used for uncomplicated cystitis; it does not penetrate the epididymis in a tissue-invasive infection.

et: Epididymitis in older men or after instrumentation
bl: In older men or after instrumentation, epididymitis is usually from enteric gram-negative rods and is treated with levofloxacin.

s: A 63-year-old man has had 3 months of dull left flank discomfort and one episode of gross hematuria. He reports a new left scrotal swelling. On standing, a soft tangle is palpable above the left testis; unlike a typical varicocele, it does not collapse when he lies down. The testes are normal. Blood pressure is 150/92 mm Hg, and hemoglobin is 18.4 g/dL.
l: Which is the most likely cause of the scrotal finding?
o: Nutcracker compression of the left renal vein
Renal cell carcinoma invading the left renal vein
e: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle, so a tumor growing into the renal vein blocks its outflow and the pampiniform plexus stays full even when he lies down. A new varicocele that does not collapse supine, especially with flank pain and hematuria in an older man, therefore suggests **renal cell carcinoma** invading the renal vein; the tumor can also make erythropoietin, which explains his high hemoglobin. A right-sided varicocele raises the same concern for inferior vena cava involvement. Nutcracker syndrome affects young, thin patients, and the other tumors do not block this venous route.

w.Nutcracker compression of the left renal: Compression of the left renal vein between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta can cause hematuria and a left varicocele, but it affects young, thin patients and does not cause erythrocytosis or a mass.
w.Testicular germ cell tumor: A testicular germ cell tumor is a painless firm intratesticular mass in a young man; it does not block venous return from the cord, and the testes are normal here.
w.Prostate adenocarcinoma: Prostate adenocarcinoma arises in the posterior gland and spreads to bone; it presents with urinary symptoms or a hard nodule, not flank discomfort with hematuria, erythrocytosis and a nonreducing varicocele.
w.Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder causes painless hematuria in smokers, but it does not obstruct the left renal vein, raise hemoglobin or produce a unilateral varicocele.

et: Nutcracker compression of the left renal vein
Left renal vein squeezed by the superior mesenteric artery
None; the mass is inside the testis
Hard prostate nodule or bone pain
Renal cell carcinoma invading the left renal vein
Tumor in the renal vein blocks testicular vein outflow
bl: A new varicocele that does not empty when lying down means blocked venous return, and in an older man it suggests renal cell carcinoma.

s: A 34-year-old man notices a painless swelling above his left testis while showering. Examination shows a smooth, 2-cm cystic mass lying above and behind the left testis, which can be felt separately from it. The mass lights up when a penlight is held against it. The testis itself is normal, and a standing examination shows no dilated veins.
l: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
e: A **spermatocele**, or epididymal cyst, is a sperm-filled cyst of the epididymis that sits above and behind the testis and can be separated from it by palpation. It contains clear fluid, so it transilluminates. A **hydrocele** also glows but surrounds the testis, so the testis cannot be felt apart from it. A varicocele is a bag of worms that does not transilluminate, a hematocele is blood that stays dark, and a germ cell tumor is solid, firm and inseparable from the testis. Spermatoceles are benign and are removed only if they cause symptoms.

w.Varicocele: A varicocele is a bag of worms of dilated pampiniform veins that fills on standing and does not transilluminate because blood blocks the light; here there are no dilated veins and the cyst glows.
w.Hematocele: A hematocele is blood in the tunica vaginalis after trauma and stays dark; this man has no injury, and his mass transilluminates.
w.Germ cell tumor: A germ cell tumor is a firm, solid intratesticular mass that cannot be separated from the testis and does not transilluminate.
w.Hydrocele: A hydrocele also transilluminates but surrounds the testis, which cannot be felt separately; this cyst lies above and behind the testis and can be separated from it.

et: In the cord, above the testis
Around the testis, inside the tunica vaginalis
bl: A spermatocele is a benign epididymal cyst above and behind the testis, separable from it, that transilluminates.

pt.say: The spermatocele row sits above and behind the testis as a sperm-filled epididymal cyst that is separate from it and glows, which distinguishes it from a hydrocele around the testis.

s: A 20-month-old boy is brought to his pediatrician because his parents noticed painless enlargement of the right testis over the past 2 months. Examination shows a firm, nontender right testicular mass that does not transilluminate. The serum alpha-fetoprotein concentration is markedly elevated, and serum hCG is normal. Histologic examination of the resected tumor shows structures that resemble primitive glomeruli.
l: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
e: A **yolk sac tumor** is the most common testicular tumor in boys younger than 3. It secretes alpha-fetoprotein and forms **Schiller-Duval bodies**, glomerulus-like structures with a central vessel ringed by tumor cells. Prepubertal yolk sac tumors have a very good prognosis. Seminoma never makes AFP and occurs in adult men, embryonal carcinoma is a hemorrhagic tumor of young adults, choriocarcinoma raises hCG rather than AFP, and teratoma shows tissues from all three germ layers.

w.Seminoma: Seminoma occurs in men in their 30s and 40s and never makes AFP; a markedly elevated AFP in a toddler excludes it.
w.Embryonal carcinoma: Embryonal carcinoma is a hemorrhagic, necrotic tumor of young adults made of pleomorphic primitive cells, and it does not form glomerulus-like structures.
w.Choriocarcinoma: Choriocarcinoma secretes very high hCG, not AFP, and consists of trophoblastic cells; this boy's hCG is normal.
w.Teratoma: Teratomas contain mature or immature tissues from all three germ layers, such as cartilage, skin and neural tissue, and would not show glomerulus-like structures with a high AFP.

et: AFP normal; hCG normal or mildly raised
Tissues of all three germ layers
bl: Yolk sac tumor is the testicular tumor of boys under 3, with high AFP and Schiller-Duval bodies.

pt.say: The yolk sac tumor box in the nonseminomatous branch lists Schiller-Duval bodies, high AFP and boys under 3, which matches the toddler with a high AFP and glomerulus-like structures.

s: A 34-year-old man undergoes radical inguinal orchiectomy for a painless left testicular mass. Histology shows sheets of large cells with clear cytoplasm and distinct borders, separated by fibrous septa containing lymphocytes. No other tumor elements are found on extensive sampling. Preoperative serum studies show an alpha-fetoprotein concentration of 420 ng/mL (normal less than 10), hCG of 30 mIU/mL (normal less than 5) and a mildly elevated lactate dehydrogenase.
l: Which interpretation of these results is most appropriate?
o: A nonseminomatous component is present despite the histology
The mildly raised hCG alone excludes a pure seminoma
A raised AFP is a usual finding in classic pure seminoma
The raised LDH proves widespread metastatic disease
Syncytiotrophoblast cells in the tumor explain both markers
e: Pure **seminoma** never makes AFP, because its cells lack yolk sac differentiation. A raised AFP therefore means that a nonseminomatous element, usually yolk sac tumor, is present even if sampling missed it, and the patient is staged and treated as having a **nonseminomatous germ cell tumor**. A mild hCG rise is compatible with seminoma, since scattered syncytiotrophoblast cells make small amounts, and LDH reflects tumor bulk rather than tumor type. The distinction matters because seminoma is highly radiosensitive, whereas nonseminomatous tumors are treated mainly with chemotherapy and surgery.

w.The mildly raised hCG alone excludes a p: Scattered syncytiotrophoblast cells in some seminomas release small amounts of hCG, so a mild rise is compatible with pure seminoma and does not exclude it.
w.A raised AFP is a usual finding in class: Pure seminoma never secretes AFP, because its cells lack yolk sac differentiation, so an elevated AFP always signals another germ cell element.
w.The raised LDH proves widespread metasta: LDH reflects tumor bulk and helps with staging in any germ cell tumor, but it is nonspecific and does not by itself prove metastasis.
w.Syncytiotrophoblast cells in the tumor e: Syncytiotrophoblast cells in seminoma can explain a mild hCG rise, but they do not secrete AFP, so they cannot account for this man's markedly elevated AFP.

et: A nonseminomatous component is present despite the histology
Only yolk sac or embryonal cells make AFP
The mildly raised hCG alone excludes a pure seminoma
Syncytiotrophoblast cells in seminoma can make mild hCG
A raised AFP is a usual finding in classic pure seminoma
The raised LDH proves widespread metastatic disease
LDH tracks tumor bulk, not tumor type
Syncytiotrophoblast cells in the tumor explain both markers
One cell type explains both markers
Syncytiotrophoblast cells make hCG, not AFP
bl: A raised AFP means a nonseminomatous component, so a tumor reported as seminoma is managed as nonseminomatous; mild hCG is compatible with seminoma.

hl: AFP raised: a nonseminomatous part is present, never pure seminoma
hCG very high: choriocarcinoma; mildly raised: seminoma is still possible
pt.say: The bottom notes state that a raised AFP means a nonseminomatous part is present, never pure seminoma, while a mildly raised hCG still allows seminoma.

s: A 38-year-old man has had 6 months of breast enlargement and tenderness and reduced libido. Examination shows bilateral gynecomastia and a 1.5-cm firm, nontender nodule in the right testis; the left testis is normal. Serum hCG and AFP are normal, serum estradiol is elevated and LH is low. Resection shows a golden-brown, well-circumscribed nodule of polygonal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm that contains rod-shaped crystalloids.
e: A golden-brown nodule of polygonal eosinophilic cells with rod-shaped **Reinke crystals** is a **Leydig cell tumor**, a sex cord-stromal tumor. It makes androgens and estrogens, so boys develop precocious puberty and adults develop gynecomastia, with suppressed LH and normal hCG and AFP. Choriocarcinoma can also cause gynecomastia, but through very high hCG, and it is hemorrhagic and made of trophoblastic cells. Seminoma and embryonal carcinoma are germ cell tumors that do not secrete steroids, and Sertoli cell tumors are usually hormonally silent.

w.Embryonal carcinoma: Embryonal carcinoma is a hemorrhagic, necrotic mass of primitive pleomorphic cells that may raise AFP or hCG; it makes no steroid hormones and has no crystalloids.
w.Seminoma: Seminoma is a pale gray-white mass of fried-egg cells with lymphocytes in fibrous septa; it does not secrete sex steroids.
w.Choriocarcinoma: Choriocarcinoma also causes gynecomastia, through very high hCG, but hCG is normal here and the tumor would be hemorrhagic with trophoblastic cells and early lung metastases.
w.Sertoli cell tumor: Sertoli cell tumors are usually hormonally silent and lack Reinke crystals; a golden-brown nodule with rod-shaped crystalloids is a Leydig cell tumor.

et: AFP normal; hCG normal or mildly raised
Cords and tubules of Sertoli cells
bl: A Leydig cell tumor with Reinke crystals makes androgens and estrogens, causing precocious puberty in boys or gynecomastia in men, with normal AFP and hCG.

pt.say: The sex cord-stromal box lists Leydig cell tumors with Reinke crystals and androgen or estrogen excess, so a golden nodule with rod-shaped crystalloids and gynecomastia fits a Leydig cell tumor.

s: A 31-year-old man has a painless, firm left testicular mass found on self-examination. At age 6 he underwent left orchiopexy for an undescended testis. Ultrasonography shows a solid, homogeneous intratesticular lesion. After radical inguinal orchiectomy, the pathologist finds a pale, fleshy tumor of uniform large cells with clear cytoplasm and lymphocytes in fibrous septa. In the adjacent seminiferous tubules, atypical large germ cells with clear cytoplasm lie along the basement membrane, confined within the tubules.
l: Which lesion in the adjacent tubules is the precursor of this tumor?
o: Atrophic tubules with a thickened basement membrane
Maturation arrest at the primary spermatocyte stage
e: Most testicular germ cell tumors, including seminoma, arise from **germ cell neoplasia in situ** (GCNIS), atypical large germ cells with clear cytoplasm that sit inside the seminiferous tubules next to the invasive tumor. Cryptorchidism reflects testicular dysgenesis, so the risk of germ cell tumor stays raised in the repaired testis and in the other testis; orchiopexy between 6 and 18 months protects fertility and allows examination but does not remove it. An undescended testis also shows tubular atrophy with a thickened basement membrane and loss of spermatogonia, but that explains infertility, not cancer. Sertoli cell-only tubules, maturation arrest and Leydig cell hyperplasia are not neoplastic precursors.

w.Sertoli cell-only tubules: Sertoli cell-only tubules lack germ cells entirely and reflect germ cell aplasia, which causes infertility with a high FSH but is not a malignant precursor; the cells here are atypical germ cells.
w.Atrophic tubules with a thickened baseme: Thickened basement membranes and loss of spermatogonia are typical of an undescended testis and explain infertility, but they are degenerative changes, not the neoplastic precursor.
w.Maturation arrest at the primary spermat: Arrest at the primary spermatocyte stage shows many early germ cells but no later forms and causes azoospermia; it is a functional block, not an atypical intratubular proliferation.
w.Leydig cell hyperplasia: Leydig cells often look prominent in an atrophic cryptorchid testis, but they sit in the interstitium and are not the atypical intratubular germ cells described here.

et: Tubules lined by Sertoli cells alone
Atrophic tubules with a thickened basement membrane
Maturation arrest at the primary spermatocyte stage
Tubules with early germ cells only
Atypical large germ cells inside tubules
bl: Germ cell neoplasia in situ is the intratubular precursor of most testicular germ cell tumors and is more frequent in cryptorchid testes.

pt.say: The germ cell branch labels GCNIS as the precursor of germ cell tumors in men aged 15 to 35, beside isochromosome 12p, so the intratubular atypical germ cells are germ cell neoplasia in situ.

s: A 27-year-old man has a 3-week history of a painless, firm right testicular mass. Ultrasonography shows a 3-cm solid hypoechoic intratesticular lesion with no hydrocele. He is afebrile and has no urinary symptoms. Blood has been drawn for AFP, hCG and LDH. He has no children and hopes to have them. His surgeon plans definitive diagnosis and treatment.
o: Transscrotal needle biopsy of the testicular mass
Scrotal orchiectomy with preservation of the cord
Observation with repeat ultrasonography in 6 weeks
Radical inguinal orchiectomy with high cord ligation
e: A solid intratesticular mass in a young man is a germ cell tumor until proven otherwise. The testis develops near the kidney, so its lymph drains to **para-aortic nodes**, whereas scrotal skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes. Entering the scrotum could spill tumor into the scrotal wall and open a second nodal route, so the testis and cord are removed through the groin by **radical inguinal orchiectomy** with high ligation of the cord. Markers are drawn first, and sperm banking is offered before treatment. Biopsy, scrotal surgery, observation and antibiotics would delay or compromise cure.

w.Transscrotal needle biopsy of the testic: Violating the scrotal wall can seed tumor into scrotal tissue and open lymphatics to the inguinal nodes, creating a second drainage route that complicates staging, so biopsy through the scrotum is avoided.
w.Scrotal orchiectomy with preservation of: Operating through the scrotum carries the same risk as a transscrotal biopsy, and leaving the cord behind leaves tumor-bearing lymphatics and vessels in place.
w.Observation with repeat ultrasonography: Waiting 6 weeks delays treatment of a presumed germ cell tumor, which is highly curable when treated early; a solid intratesticular mass is not expected to resolve.
w.Empiric antibiotics for presumed epididy: Antibiotics treat epididymo-orchitis, which is painful and gradual with inflammation and increased flow; this painless solid mass is cancer until proven otherwise.

et: Transscrotal needle biopsy of the testicular mass
Opens scrotal lymphatics toward the inguinal nodes
Scrotal orchiectomy with preservation of the cord
Same risk, and the cord is left behind
Observation with repeat ultrasonography in 6 weeks
Radical inguinal orchiectomy with high cord ligation
Keeps drainage to para-aortic nodes only
bl: A suspected testicular tumor is removed by radical inguinal orchiectomy, never by scrotal biopsy, to avoid spread to the inguinal nodes.

pt.say: The top of the figure shows a painless, firm intratesticular mass that spreads to para-aortic nodes, so the testis and cord are removed through the groin by radical inguinal orchiectomy to keep the scrotal lymphatics untouched.

s: A 19-year-old man who never received routine childhood vaccines had parotid swelling and a low-grade fever 6 days ago. He now has a temperature of 38.7 °C and a swollen, exquisitely tender right testis with reddened scrotal skin. The testis and epididymis cannot be separated on palpation, and urinalysis is normal. Eight months later, ultrasonography shows a small, atrophic right testis.
l: Which mechanism best explains the atrophy of the testis?
o: Pressure necrosis of tubules within the tunica albuginea
Direct viral destruction of Leydig cells
Bacterial abscess formation within the epididymis
Venous obstruction from torsion of the spermatic cord
Heat injury from loss of pampiniform cooling
e: Mumps is the classic cause of viral **orchitis**, inflaming the testis in roughly 20 to 30 percent of males infected after puberty, usually about a week after parotitis. The inflamed testis swells inside the tough, inelastic **tunica albuginea**, so pressure rises and compresses the seminiferous tubules and their blood supply, causing pressure necrosis and atrophy. Damage to the blood-testis barrier adds an immune attack, and bilateral disease can cause infertility. The tubules suffer more than the Leydig cells, the process is sterile rather than bacterial, and torsion would start abruptly with an absent cremasteric reflex.

w.Direct viral destruction of Leydig cells: Mumps orchitis damages the tubules more than the interstitium; Leydig cells are relatively spared, so sperm production is lost more often than androgen production.
w.Bacterial abscess formation within the e: Mumps is viral and the orchitis is sterile inflammation with edema and lymphocytes; the epididymis is not the site of an abscess here, and the urinalysis shows no pyuria.
w.Venous obstruction from torsion of the s: Torsion begins abruptly in an adolescent with an absent cremasteric reflex; this man has a preceding viral illness with parotitis, redness and a gradual course.
w.Heat injury from loss of pampiniform coo: The pampiniform plexus continues to cool arterial blood in orchitis; the damage comes from inflammation and trapped swelling, not from loss of heat exchange.

et: Pressure necrosis of tubules within the tunica albuginea
Direct viral destruction of Leydig cells
Not the main injury in mumps
Bacterial abscess formation within the epididymis
Venous obstruction from torsion of the spermatic cord
Heat injury from loss of pampiniform cooling
bl: Mumps orchitis damages the tubules because swelling is trapped inside the unyielding tunica albuginea, causing pressure necrosis and atrophy.

s: A 26-year-old man has had 2 months of palpitations, weight loss, heat intolerance and enlarging, tender breasts. He has had episodes of hemoptysis. Examination shows a heart rate of 112/min, a fine tremor, bilateral gynecomastia and a small firm mass in the left testis. Serum TSH is suppressed with an elevated free thyroxine, and TSH-receptor antibodies are negative. Chest imaging shows multiple bilateral nodules. Serum hCG is extremely high.
l: Which tumor is the most likely cause of his findings?
e: **Choriocarcinoma** is made of syncytiotrophoblast and cytotrophoblast and secretes very high levels of hCG. hCG resembles TSH enough to stimulate the TSH receptor weakly, causing hyperthyroidism with suppressed TSH, and its stimulation of Leydig cells to make estrogen causes gynecomastia. The tumor often has a small primary and spreads early through the blood to the lungs, which explains the hemoptysis and nodules. Seminoma raises hCG only mildly, yolk sac tumor makes AFP, embryonal carcinoma is hemorrhagic with variable markers, and Leydig cell tumors leave hCG normal.

w.Embryonal carcinoma: Embryonal carcinoma may raise hCG or AFP modestly, but it is a hemorrhagic tumor of primitive cells and does not usually reach hCG levels high enough to cause thyrotoxicosis with early lung metastases.
w.Yolk sac tumor: Yolk sac tumor secretes AFP and occurs mainly in young boys; it does not cause extreme hCG elevation.
w.Seminoma: Seminoma can raise hCG only mildly through scattered syncytiotrophoblast cells, and it spreads mainly through lymphatics; extreme hCG with early lung metastases is not its pattern.
w.Leydig cell tumor: Leydig cell tumors cause gynecomastia through estrogen excess, but hCG and AFP stay normal, and hyperthyroidism and lung metastases would not be expected.

et: AFP normal; hCG normal or mildly raised
bl: Choriocarcinoma makes very high hCG, which causes gynecomastia and hyperthyroidism and spreads early through the blood to the lungs.

pt.say: The choriocarcinoma box shows trophoblast cells, very high hCG and blood spread to the lungs, which matches the gynecomastia, thyrotoxicosis, hemoptysis and lung nodules.

s: A 72-year-old man notices painless enlargement of both testes over 4 months, with night sweats and a 6-kg weight loss. Examination shows firm, nontender, enlarged testes bilaterally and no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Serum AFP and hCG are normal. Ultrasonography shows diffuse hypoechoic enlargement of both testes.
l: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
e: In men older than 60, the most common testicular mass is **lymphoma**, usually diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and it is often bilateral. It causes painless diffuse enlargement, and constitutional symptoms such as night sweats and weight loss fit lymphoma. Germ cell tumors peak in younger men, produce AFP or hCG in several types and are usually unilateral, so normal markers and bilateral enlargement in a 72-year-old shift the diagnosis. Leydig cell tumors secrete hormones and form discrete nodules.

w.Seminoma: Seminoma is usually a unilateral tumor of men in their 30s and 40s; bilateral involvement, age 72 and night sweats are not its pattern.
w.Leydig cell tumor: Leydig cell tumors are small unilateral nodules that secrete hormones, causing gynecomastia in adults; this man has bilateral diffuse enlargement and no hormonal features.
w.Embryonal carcinoma: Embryonal carcinoma occurs in men in their 20s and 30s as a hemorrhagic mass and often raises AFP or hCG, neither of which fits.
w.Yolk sac tumor: Yolk sac tumor affects boys under 3 and makes AFP; it would not appear in a 72-year-old with a normal AFP.

et: AFP normal; hCG normal or mildly raised
AFP and hCG normal; hormones raised

s: A 14-year-old boy undergoes emergency surgery 14 hours after the sudden onset of severe left scrotal pain. The spermatic cord is twisted two full turns, and the testis is swollen and dark purple-black. It does not regain color after detorsion, and orchiectomy is performed. Histology shows interstitial hemorrhage, congested vessels and coagulative necrosis of the seminiferous tubules.
l: Which sequence of vascular events best explains these findings?
o: Thick-walled arteries close first, so the testis becomes pale and ischemic
Thin-walled veins close first, so the testis congests and then infarcts
Veins and arteries close together, so a pale infarct forms at once
Lymphatics close first, so edema develops without infarction
Venous thrombosis develops first as infection spreads along the cord
e: In **testicular torsion**, the twisted spermatic cord compresses the thin-walled, low-pressure veins before the thicker, higher-pressure arteries. Blood therefore still enters the testis but cannot leave, so the organ becomes engorged and dark, and prolonged venous congestion raises tissue pressure until arterial flow fails and the testis undergoes **hemorrhagic infarction** rather than a pale one. Salvage is high within 6 hours and low after 24. An early arterial block would give a pale infarct, simultaneous occlusion is not the usual sequence, and lymphatic obstruction or infection does not explain this picture.

w.Thick-walled arteries close first, so th: Arteries have thick walls and high pressure, so they resist compression longer than veins; closing them first would give a pale, ischemic testis rather than the dark, congested one seen here.
w.Veins and arteries close together, so a: Simultaneous occlusion would starve the tissue of blood without congestion, producing a pale infarct, whereas this testis is engorged with blood and hemorrhagic.
w.Lymphatics close first, so edema develop: Lymphatic blockage causes edema, but it cannot explain hemorrhage and coagulative necrosis of the tubules, which require venous congestion and then loss of arterial inflow.
w.Venous thrombosis develops first as infe: Septic venous thrombosis would follow an infection with fever and pyuria; this boy had sudden pain with a twisted cord, and detorsion revealed the mechanical cause.

pt.say: The bell-clapper panel shows the twisted cord with thin-walled veins closing first, followed by congestion and hemorrhagic infarction, which explains the dark swollen testis.
